Rational functions. A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials, written as f of x equals P of x divided by Q of x, where both numerator and denominator are polynomials. Rational functions generalize simpler polynomial behavior by introducing asymptotes and discontinuities, making them essential in modeling rates, proportions, and complex engineering systems.

The general form is f of x equals P of x divided by Q of x, where P and Q are polynomials and Q is not the zero polynomial. Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero and the numerator is nonzero. The function approaches infinity near these points. Horizontal asymptotes are determined by comparing the degrees of P and Q. If the degree of P is less than the degree of Q, the horizontal asymptote is y equals zero. If the degrees are equal, the horizontal asymptote is y equals the ratio of the leading coefficients. If the degree of P exceeds the degree of Q, there is no horizontal asymptote. An oblique or slant asymptote appears when the degree of P is exactly one more than the degree of Q. You find it by polynomial long division. Rational functions are continuous except at the zeros of Q, and they're differentiable wherever they are continuous. Common examples include one divided by x, the reciprocal function, one divided by x squared, and the rational function x plus one divided by x minus two. Understanding the asymptotic behavior is key to graphing rational functions and predicting their behavior at extreme values.
